Annotated Kanji Table

※ Explanation

Kanji table containing all 6527 Kanji that are at leat one of:

  • Included in Unicode Unihan Core 2020 with a J source (6490)
  • Included in Unicode IRG IICore with J source (4600) (mostly a subset of the above, save for 20 Kanji that were not included in Unihan Core 2020)
  • Included in the Publishing Kanji list (表外漢字字体表, see Grade 12 and V descriptions below), including simplified common forms (簡易慣用字体) (1022).
  • Variant Kanji that at one point had the same JIS encoding as any Jōyō, Jinmeiyō or Publishing Kanji (表外漢字字体表)-included Kanji or are JIS X 0208 variants of JIS Level 3 Kanji in the above (62).
  • Regularly used for spelling entries included in JMdict (see dictionary level 1-4 below) (3879).
All 1026 Kyōiku, 1110 further Jōyō and 863 Jinmeiyō Kanji are covered by this as of 2025.

The table is ordered by Grade, then by JIS level, then by JIS Ku-ten code (Kanji outside JIS follow afterwards inside that final ordering level, ordered by Unicode code point).

Column 級/Kyu indicates the grade of the Kanji. Grades 1-10 are according to the EDRDG KANJIDIC2 data, the grades beyond that are specific to this table.

  • Grades 1-6 are the 1026 Kyōiku Kanji of that grade level (Kyōiku Kanji).
  • Grade 8 are the remaining 1110 Jōyō Kanji.
  • Grade 9 and 10 are the 863 Jinmeiyō Kanji. Grade 9 are those 651 that are not variants of any Jōyō Kanji, and grade 10 the remaining 212 Jinmeiyō Kanji.
  • Grade 12 are 514 Hyōgai Kanji listed as standard printed forms (印刷標準字体) in the 表外漢字字体表 (Publishing Kanji list). Simplified common forms (簡易慣用字体) from the same list are in grade V instead. See also ₚ grade indicator.
  • V are 62 Hyōgai Kanji which are close variants of any of the Kanji listed in the grades above, either they once had the same JIS encoding (i variant) with a related Kanji that has grade 1-12, or it corresponds to a Kanji added specifically as a standard printed form variant in the 2004 extension of JIS X 0213, or it is listed as a simplified common form (簡易慣用字体) in the Publishing Kanji list (表外漢字字体表). i-variants without such a graded counterpart are included in their natural non-V grade.
  • Ha are 504 other Hyōgai Kanji guessed to be common.
  • Finally, Hb (905) and Hc (1543) are the remaining 2448 included Hyōgai Kanji, this should constitute less common Hyōgai Kanji, although especially those in the Hb grade may still be of some relevance.
  • Grade numbers 7 and 11 are not defined.

Furthermore, the Grade column can have any of these indicators indicating their history:

  • No indicator: The Kanji was already first listed as Jinmeiyō or Tōyō Kanji (precedessor of Jōyō Kanji) before 1981 and was never removed from these lists.
  • ': The Kanji is an alternative form (typically Kyūjitai) that was at some point only in the additional list of characters acceptable in personal names (人名用漢字許容字体表) which was established in 1981 and merged into the Jinmeiyō Kanji in 2004. A few of these were earlier Jinmeiyō Kanji (namely 亙琢渚龍) and one (燈) a Tōyō Kanji. The rest have never been included in either of these lists until 2004. As the list was never modified between 1981 and 2004, this indicator never occurs in combination with another.
  • ⁰: Current Jōyō Kanji that were former Jinmeiyō Kanji, first listed before in 1951 (introduction of Jinmeiyō list) or 1976.
  • ¹: First listed in 1981 with expansion of Tōyō to Jōyō.
  • ²: First listed in 1990 or 1997 (Jinmeiyō).
  • ³: First listed in 2004 (Jinmeiyō).
  • ⁴: First listed in 2009 (Jinmeiyō), 2010 (Jōyō), 2015 (Jinmeiyō) or 2017 (Jinmeiyō).
  • ₚ: Listed in the Publishing Kanji list (表外漢字字体表, 2000). The Kanji on that list that are still Hyōgai are listed as grade 12 without a redundant ₚ, with the exception of simplified common forms (簡易慣用字体) listed in the Publishing Kanji list (表外漢字字体表), which are listed under grade V but marked Vₚ. Mostly this mark appears on Kanji included as Jōyō or Jinmeiyō Kanji afterwards; in that case it always occurs in combination with ³ or ⁴.
The 準/Jun column describes the JIS Level of the Kanji which is usually 1-4, with Levels 1-2 according to JIS X 0208 (6355 included Kanji), level 3-4 according to JIS X 0213 (166 included Kanji). JIS X 0213 (2000, revised 2004) is the later extension/successor of JIS X 0208, while JIS X 0212 (1990) is a separate supplementary set intended for use together with JIS X 0208 and is now mostly obsolete. Kanji contained only in JIS X 0213 level 3-4 but not JIS X 0212 have an asterisk * after the level. Level 0 indicates Kanji contained in JIS X 0208 but outside Kanji rows. Level 5 indicates Kanji only in JIS X 0212, Level 6 indicates Kanji not in any of these JIS standards but in the Unicode Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP). Kanji in Level 1-3 that have a ' appended to the level have had their canonical appearance modified in the 2004 to JIS X 0213, level 3 Kanji with a " appended are wholly new from that 2004 revision. " can also appear in level 2, in which case the Ku-Ten code was added after the original 1978 revision of JIS X 0208, i.e. neither the Kanji nor a variant form with the same JIS encoding (see i-Variant below) were specified back then.

The C/Core column contains the priority in IICore. It is uppercase if has the J source there, and lowercase for any other Kanji in IICore, or a dash if it's not in IICore. If the Kanji is not in Unihan Core 2020, there is a circle (°) after the IICore priority, if it is in Unhihan Core 2020 but without J source, there is an asterisk. Furthermore, a ' is appended if the Kanji is outside the CJK Unified Ideographs Unicode Block (URO) and a " if it wholly outside the BMP.

The 辞/Ji column contains a "dictionary level" based on EDRDG JMDict. 1 are the 482 Kanji that are particularly common. 2 (1608) and 3 (490) are Kanji that are less common but still above average. 4 are 1299 Kanji that regularly occur but are not really common. 5 are 1097 Kanji that have only one or two entries regularly spelled with that Kanji but no more. After that, 6 are 417 Kanji only occuring in rare or obsolete spellings or at most two regular spellings, 7 are 107 Kanji only in irregular spellings (includes spellings marked as search-only). There are 1027 further included Kanji that do not appear in JMDict-listed spellings at all, marked with a dash.

Colum Vars/Variants contains variants of the Kanji listed in either the Unicode Unihan database, the EDRDG KANJIDIC2 data or (partially) en.wiktionary.org. The variant Kanji (or other Han character) is listed first and then any single-letter variant indicators indicating the kind(s) or source(s) of that variant. Hover with the mouse over the indidator letter for more information. Note that the Unicode data seems to be focused more on Chinese than Japanese. The variant Kanji are colored according to their Grade level (see above). If a Kanji/Han character is not included in the table at all, it is faded in a lighter shade of grey than the lowercase h-graded Kanji.

  • j, 2, 3, u: Variant listed in KANJIDIC2 as JIS X 0208, JIS X 0212, JIS X 0213 or Unicode variant respectively. This data is a bit messy, e.g. multiple redundant variant codes may be present or a variant that is actually in JIS X 0208 may be listed only as Unicode variant. The kind of relation is also not clearly defined but most often it is a quite close variant such as Shinjitai/Kyūjitai or another style variant.
  • n: Variant listed in KANJIDIC2 as Nelson dictionary variant. Often these are related characters that share some common meaning and reading but are not interchangeable (or at least exchanging them changes the nuance).
  • z: Variant listed in Unicode as kZVariant ("z-variant"), i.e. a purely stylistic variant with identical meaning.
  • C: A Kajji for which this indicator appears is not considered a proper (unified) Han character by Unicode but merely a CJK compatibility character. The indicated variant is the "proper" character. This represents the Unicode kCompatibilityVariant property.
  • J: This variant indicator only appears for Jinmeiyō Kanji that the Japanese authorities consider (less standard) variants and the variant with the J indicator is the "more proper" one. In particular, by definition, all "grade 10" Jinmeiyō will have such a variant and it will be a Jōyō kanji. The data stems from the Unicode property kJinmeiyoKanji. For "grade 9" Jinmeiyō, it sometimes states the opposite of Unicode's opinion of of what the proper character should be as indicated by the C/kCompatibilityVariant variant.
  • Ĵ: This variant indicator only appears rarely for Hyōgai Kanji in JIS X 0208 (i.e. JIS level 1 or 2) that are considered acceptable variants of Jōyō kanji which are outside JIS X 0208. The data stems from the Unicode kJoyoKanji property.
  • y, m: Variant listed in Unicode as kSemanticVariant (y) or kSpecializedSemanticVariant (m). Note that these can be totally wrong for Japanese usage as the Unicode data seems to be more Chinese-focused.
  • t, s: Unicode kTraditionalVariant and kSimplifiedVariant. This is mostly not useful for Japanese usage as it relates to Chinese.
  • x: Unicode kSpoofingVariant. Looks (probably) deceptively similar but might be completely unrelated in meaning.
  • ẋ: Unicode confusable. Looks deceptively similar but might be completely unrelated in meaning. This does not include all confusables but only single-codepoint Han characters, excluding any compatibility variants that are neither in KANJIDIC 2 nor have a Unihan kIRG_JSource property (not having that property indicates no usage in any Japanese source).
  • D: en.wiktionary.org-sourced data indicating that the row Kanji (non-Tōyō) has mostly fallen out of modern use in favor of the Tōyō Kanji indicated as variant. Corresponds to Template:ja-toyo-depre.
  • k, e, o: en.wiktionary.org-sourced data indicating a Japanese form (k, usually Shinjitai), extended Shinjitai (e) and Kyūjitai/traditional/old form (o). Sometimes wrong data may appear here as Wiktionary references multiple forms that correspond to the same Chinese-simplified form on the same page inside the same box/template even if they are not related at all in Japanese usage and the data extraction method used is not smart enough to handle that.
  • i: Variant Kanji form that occupied the same JIS X 0208 code at some point. Consequently a Kanji beyond level 2 (outside JIS X 0208) that has an level 1-2 i variant was once present in JIS X 0208 and a ⁰ indicator will be added to the level (for example JIS X 0213 level 3 Kanji 1-89-35 "禱" was at JIS X 0208 1-37-88 until before the 1983 revision of the standard, when it was replaced by the Shinjitai variant 祷, so both Kanji have an i-Variant pointing to each other). This information is sourced from the Adobe-Japan-1 detailed Kanji information file (a17-kanji.txt) which is organized by Glyph (visible character form identified by a CID) and has various versions of JIS as well as Unicode encodings for each.
  • r: A reverse variant indicator. This means that the variant Kanji has at least one variant entry pointing to this Kanji, but not the other way round.
  • b: Variant indicator for Kanji that share similar/same parts.
  • !, °: An exclamation mark refers to a Kanji that is the primary variant, meaning that it is more common and can act as replacement in most contexts. This is typically a Shinjitai/Kyūjitai pair, with the ! indicating the more common variant (most often but not always the Shinjitai). There is at most one such variant per Kanji. A Kanji that has such a variant is considered a secondary variant and will be displayed in faded colors in its main row. A degree symbol ° is used on the other side, i.e. it indicates a close variant that is less common than this Kanji. This is purely derived based on other variant-relations so it is not a real variant indicator but an annotation of another. Currently, variant relations j, 2, 3, u, D, k, e, o, z, J, Ĵ and C are considered such close variants, while others are ignored for the purpose of the !/° relation.
  • V:: Pseudo-variant. The same unicode code point as the row kanji but with different Adobe variation selectors. Usually before/after the 2004 JIS update related to the Publishing Kanji list (表外漢字字体表).
  • I:: Pseudo-variant added to Kanji which are encoded as CJK compatibility character in Unicode (see C variant above). Displays the same Kanji as the main row Kanji but using a combination of the Unicode code point for the corresponding Unified Han character plus a Unicode variant selector. This can be used as a workaround for copy-pasting to software where the compatibility character does not work (but overall is not less likely to have issues than the compatibility character)

Colunm Comps contains the top-level component decomposition (data from kanjivg.tagaini.net/) related to b-variants.
